title: Timeouts & Retries
subtitle: Watch a checkout service survive a flaky payment API, then watch careless retries knock that API over.
learn: How to pick a timeout from observed latency instead of guessing
How exponential backoff with jitter spaces retries out
Why layered retries multiply load into a retry storm
How retry budgets and deadlines cap the damage
Which failures are safe to retry and which are not

steps.title: The payment API gets flaky
steps.body: A checkout service calls a payment API to charge cards. Normally it answers in about 80 ms. The p99 (the slowest 1 in 100 calls) is 400 ms. Today about 30 percent of calls fail or hang, so 3 in 10 charges go wrong. Should checkout wait forever, give up at once, or try again? Each choice has a cost, and this lesson walks through them.
steps.idea: Any call over a network can be slow, fail, or never answer, so the caller needs a plan for each case.
steps.caption: Checkout depends on a payment API that now fails 3 calls in 10.

steps.title: Set a timeout first
steps.body: Without a timeout, a hung call holds a thread and a connection for as long as the OS allows, maybe minutes or forever. Enough hung calls and checkout itself runs out of threads. A timeout caps the wait: here checkout gives up at 500 ms and frees its thread. A common rule of thumb is a little above the dependency's p99 (400 ms here), then adjust from real data. Too low aborts calls that would have worked. Also set a shorter connect timeout (100-200 ms) for just opening the connection. Attempts x timeout, plus backoff, must fit the overall deadline.
steps.idea: A timeout turns an unbounded wait into a bounded one. Base it on measured p99, not on hope.
steps.caption: Checkout stops waiting at 500 ms and frees its thread.

steps.title: Retry the transient failure
steps.body: Many failures are brief: a dropped packet, a restarting server, a moment of overload. So trying again often works. (Retrying a charge safely needs idempotency, covered later.) If each attempt fails 30 percent of the time, independently, all three attempts fail only 0.3 x 0.3 x 0.3, about 3 percent. Success climbs from 70 to about 97 percent. This only works when the cause is temporary: a dead service fails every time. Retries also cost load. A call averages 1 + 0.3 + 0.09 = 1.39 attempts, so 600 req/s becomes about 834.
steps.idea: Retries convert short-lived faults into successes, but only if the next attempt has a real chance of working.
steps.caption: A second attempt reaches the Payment API and succeeds.

steps.title: Back off exponentially
steps.body: Retrying instantly hammers a service that is already struggling. Exponential backoff waits longer after each failure, doubling the gap: 100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms, 800 ms, up to a cap such as 2 seconds. In the animation, the second try waits 100 ms and the third waits 200 ms. The growing gap gives the service room to recover. Pair backoff with a maximum number of attempts, because waiting longer alone does not stop a caller from retrying forever.
steps.idea: Doubling the wait after every failure gives a struggling service breathing room.
steps.caption: Each retry waits twice as long as the previous one.

steps.title: Add jitter
steps.body: Suppose the payment API blips for one second and 5,000 callers all fail together. With plain backoff they all retry at exactly 100 ms, then all at 200 ms, hitting the service in synchronized waves. Jitter adds randomness. With full jitter each caller sleeps a random time between 0 and its current backoff value. In the animation, retries arrive at different moments (+37 ms, +64 ms, +91 ms), spreading into a smooth trickle instead of spikes.
steps.idea: Jitter breaks up synchronized retry waves; always add it to backoff.
steps.caption: Many callers retry at random moments instead of all at once.

steps.title: The retry storm
steps.body: Now the payment API is truly overloaded. It normally handles about 1,000 requests per second, but its capacity has halved to about 500. Callers time out and retry. Worse, the client app and checkout each allow 3 attempts, so one user tap can become up to 9 calls to payment (3 x 3). Normal load of 600 req/s can balloon to as much as 5,400, about ten times what payment can serve. That extra load slows payment further and causes even more retries. The helper has become the attacker, called a retry storm.
steps.idea: Retries at every layer multiply: 3 attempts across 2 layers is up to 9 calls per user action.
steps.caption: Layered retries pile load onto the already struggling Payment API.

steps.title: Cap it with a retry budget
steps.body: A retry budget caps retries as a share of total traffic, for example no more than 10 percent of recent requests may be retries. It is often built as a token bucket: each first attempt earns a fraction of a token and each retry spends one. When the bucket is empty, the call fails right away (fail fast). The price is that some calls a retry would have rescued now fail, so success only edges up from 70 to about 77 percent, not 97. But in a real outage load rises just 10 percent, so the service can recover.
steps.idea: A retry budget puts a hard ceiling on extra load no matter how many things fail.
steps.caption: Once the budget is spent, checkout fails fast instead of retrying.

steps.title: Retry only what is safe, within a deadline
steps.body: Retry only errors that may pass: connection errors, timeouts, 502, 503, 504 and 429 (honour a Retry-After hint). Never retry 400, 403 or 404, because the same request fails again. A timeout on a write leaves it unknown whether the work happened, so retrying a charge can bill twice unless it carries an idempotency key (see the Idempotency lesson). Also give the whole user action a deadline, say 2 seconds, and pass the time left downstream so no layer keeps retrying after the user left. Three 500 ms attempts plus 300 ms of backoff is about 1.8 s, which nearly fills that deadline.
steps.idea: Retry only transient, safe errors, and stop when the overall deadline runs out.
steps.caption: The time left shrinks as the request moves downstream.

steps.title: A safe retry recipe
steps.body: A safe retry recipe: set a timeout near p99. Retry only temporary errors, with exponential backoff and full jitter. Retry at one layer, not every layer. Cap retries with a budget of about 10 percent, and bound the whole thing with a deadline. Done well, retries hide small faults. Done badly, they turn a small fault into an outage.
steps.idea: Timeouts bound the wait, backoff and jitter space retries, and budgets and deadlines bound the damage.
steps.caption: All pieces together keep the system stable when payment stumbles.

quiz.q: Backoff starts at 100 ms and doubles each time, with full jitter. Roughly how long might a caller wait before its 3rd retry?
options: A random time between 0 and 400 ms
A random time between 400 and 800 ms
A random time between 0 and 100 ms
quiz.why: The delays are 100, 200, then 400 ms before the 3rd retry. Full jitter picks a random value between 0 and that ceiling.

quiz.q: A user taps Pay. The app, the checkout service and the payment API each make up to 3 attempts to the layer below it, ending at the payments database. How many calls can reach the database in the worst case?
quiz.why: Attempts multiply across layers: 3 x 3 x 3 = 27. This is why retries should usually happen at only one layer.

quiz.q: Which failure is the best candidate for an automatic retry?
options: A 503 response from an idempotent GET request
A 400 response saying the card number is malformed
A 404 for an order id that does not exist
A 403 because the API key is revoked
quiz.why: A 503 is often temporary, so a later attempt may succeed. The other errors are caused by the request or credentials and will fail the same way every time.

quiz.q: Traffic is 1,000 requests per second and the dependency is completely down. With a retry budget of 10 percent, at most about how many calls per second can it receive?
quiz.why: Retries are capped at about 10 percent of first attempts, so the total cannot exceed roughly 1,100 (1,000 first attempts plus about 100 retries). Without a budget, 3 attempts each would send about 3,000.

quiz.q: Why does a timeout set far below the dependency's p99 cause trouble?
options: It makes backoff delays too long
It aborts calls that would have succeeded and triggers extra retries
It makes the connect timeout longer than the request timeout
quiz.why: If the timeout is under p99, a large share of healthy but slow calls get cancelled and retried, which adds load and wastes the work already done.

cheatsheet.def: Maximum time to wait for a reply. Set the request timeout slightly above the dependency's measured p99, use a shorter connect timeout, and set both on every network call. Attempts x timeout plus backoff must fit the deadline.
Wait base x 2^(n-1) before retry n (n = 1, 2, 3...), up to a cap. Example: 100, 200, 400, 800 ms, capped near 2 s.
Sleep a random time between 0 and the current backoff ceiling. Spreads out synchronized retries from many callers.
Retries add load to a struggling service, which fails more calls, which causes more retries. Layered retries multiply it.
A cap on retries as a share of traffic, often about 10 percent. Past the cap, fail fast instead of retrying.
One time limit for the whole user action, passed downstream so each layer knows how much time is left.

Retry timeouts, connection errors, 429 (honour Retry-After), 502, 503 and 504 only when the operation is idempotent or carries an idempotency key. Do not retry other 4xx errors such as 400, 403 and 404.
